strengths: Clear and meaningful novelty: the paper presents, to the best of reviewer knowledge, the first framework that can ingest NeRFs of different architectures (and architectures unseen at training time) by processing their weights, combining Graph Meta-Networks (Lim et al., 2024) with the nf2vec representation learning framework.

Well-motivated and insightful empirical analysis: the t-SNE study showing that a rendering loss alone produces architecture-clustered embeddings, and that the SigLIP contrastive objective is needed for architecture-invariance, is a convincing and well-explained finding that directly connects the loss design to the desired latent-space property.

Comprehensive experimental design: the paper separates multi-architecture and single-architecture settings, evaluates classification and (instance- and class-level) retrieval, includes unseen-architecture test sets (MLP-2L, MLP-32H, TRI-2L, TRI-32H, TRI-16W, TRI-8C) with sensible variations, and provides useful ablations over the three loss variants (LR, LR+C, LC).

In the single-architecture setting, the method is shown to outperform existing specialized frameworks (nf2vec, Cardace et al.), demonstrating that the proposed general solution does not sacrifice performance.

Reproducibility appears reasonable: implementation details (encoder/decoder architecture, training hyper-parameters, hardware, training time) are documented in the appendix, and the framework is built on existing public codebases.
Honest limitations discussion: the authors explicitly acknowledge that validation is limited to two non-state-of-the-art NeRF architectures and that hash-based encodings were not tested.
weaknesses: Limited architectural diversity: despite claims of 'arbitrary architectures', experiments cover only plain MLPs and tri-planes, both small and non-SOTA. The practically important hash-grid encodings (Instant-NGP, Zip-NeRF) are untested, so generality to more complex/modern architectures (including weight sharing) remains an open question.

The instance-level retrieval results are quite weak in absolute terms (29.0–45.5% recall@1), which suggests the architecture-invariance objective is only partially effective; the paper acknowledges this but the practical value of the contrastive solution may be limited.

Some evaluation gaps: the number of NeRF architectures is small and the 'unseen architecture' variations are modest perturbations of the two families rather than genuinely different designs; there is no baseline comparison for unseen-architecture generalization beyond ablations of the proposed losses, and no baseline such as rendering-based embedding pipelines (render + image encoder) that could contextualize the weight-processing approach.

The contrastive loss requires paired NeRFs of the same object across architectures at training time, which is a non-trivial data requirement not discussed in terms of scalability or availability in real datasets.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the encoder (GMN), decoder (nf2vec), and contrastive loss (SigLIP) are all existing components; the contribution is primarily their combination plus the empirical insight about loss behavior, which is valuable but incremental.
Only synthetic ShapeNetRender data is used; robustness on real-world NeRF datasets or scenes is unaddressed.

Minor issues: a typo in the related work ('nf2vec is en encoder-decoder...'), and the choice of batch size 8 for the SigLIP loss, which is far below the regime for which SigLIP was designed, is not analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and relevant limitation of prior work (nf2vec, Cardace et al.), namely the inability to process NeRFs with architectures different from a fixed, predefined one; the resulting capability (multi-architecture and unseen-architecture inference) is new to this line of research.

The experimental design is systematic: the authors carefully separate single- vs multi-architecture settings, ablate the rendering and contrastive losses, and construct six additional unseen-architecture test sets, providing useful insights (e.g., reducing hidden dimension is more disruptive than reducing layer count).

The paper is well written and clearly structured, with an honest analysis of the limitations of each loss variant (including the fact that L_R alone performs best in many settings) and candid acknowledgment that the validated architectures are not state-of-the-art.
Reproducibility details are adequate: architectures, hyperparameters, training schedules, hardware, and dataset composition are all specified.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the paper is essentially a combination of three existing components — the GMN encoder from Lim et al. (2024), the nf2vec decoder and training pipeline, and the SigLIP loss from Zhai et al. (2023). No new architecture, theory, or algorithmic contribution is introduced; the contrastive loss for cross-architecture alignment is a fairly standard application of existing contrastive machinery.

Restricted empirical validation: experiments cover only two NeRF architectures (MLP and tri-plane) on a single synthetic dataset (ShapenetRender), both inherited from the compared baselines. The authors themselves admit hash-grid architectures (Instant-NGP, Zip-NeRF), which are the ones practitioners actually use, are untested. Generalization to 'arbitrary architectures' therefore remains largely a claim.

The central claim of an 'architecture-agnostic latent space' is not convincingly achieved: the t-SNE analysis (Figure 3, middle) shows residual architecture-based sub-clusters even with the combined loss, and the contrastive objective actually hurts classification in most multi-architecture settings (Table 1, 3). The contrastive loss mainly pays off in retrieval tasks.

Absolute performance of the flagship capability is modest: instance-level cross-architecture retrieval recall@1 tops out at ~29-45%, which is far from practically useful; the paper acknowledges the task is 'far from being solved' without offering a path forward.

The comparison against baselines is somewhat weak: nf2vec and Cardace et al. cannot be applied in the multi-architecture setting by construction, so the multi-architecture results are self-competing; in the single-architecture setting the wins over baselines are small (~1 point on MLP, and the method actually loses to Cardace et al. on several unseen tri-plane variants, Table 4).

No efficiency analysis is provided despite the motivation that weight-based processing avoids rendering: GMN encoding of tri-plane parameter graphs (with spatial nodes connected to all channel nodes) likely scales poorly, and training takes ~2 weeks on a single GPU; rendering-based baselines are never quantitatively compared in terms of time or accuracy.

Scalability and broader applicability of the parameter-graph construction to more complex architectures (weight sharing, hash tables, attention) is discussed only qualitatively and remains unverified.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to perform downstream tasks on NeRF weights in a way that is agnostic to the underlying architecture and generalizes to architectures unseen at training time, filling a genuine gap between nf2vec-style NeRF processing and the graph meta-network literature.

The empirical finding that a rendering loss alone induces architecture-separated clusters (Figure 3, left) is an interesting and non-obvious observation, and the motivation for the SigLIP contrastive term follows logically from it; the t-SNE analyses are informative and honest (e.g., showing LR+C is not fully architecture-agnostic).

The evaluation is thorough for a first method in this setting: multi-architecture and single-architecture settings, classification and instance/class-level retrieval, and a carefully constructed suite of unseen-architecture test sets (varying hidden layers, hidden dims, tri-plane resolution and channels) with per-variant analysis of failure modes.
The method outperforms existing single-architecture baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) even in their own restricted settings (Table 2), showing it is competitive rather than merely more flexible.

The paper is clearly written, the method section is detailed, and reproducibility information (architectures, hyperparameters, training time, hardware, codebases used) is provided in the appendix; limitations are candidly acknowledged in the conclusion.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is largely compositional: the encoder is a re-adaptation of the GMN from Lim et al. (2024), the decoder and rendering loss are taken from nf2vec (Zama Ramirez et al., 2024), and the contrastive objective is SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023). The core contribution is the combination and the empirical study rather than a new architectural or algorithmic idea, which limits impact.

The claimed 'any architecture' generality is validated on only two fairly similar hybrid families (MLPs and tri-plane+MLP), both on synthetic ShapeNetRender data with the same underlying scenes. Critically, the hash-grid-based architectures (Instant-NGP/Zip-NeRF) that the authors themselves admit are what practitioners actually use are not tested, and these are precisely where parameter-graph construction (weight sharing, many hash table entries) would be most challenging.

No comparison against a simple rendering-based baseline (e.g., rendering images from NeRFs and feeding them to a standard image encoder) is provided, even though this is described as the 'naive solution'; such a baseline would help quantify the practical benefit of weight-space processing, particularly for unseen architectures.

Instance-level retrieval performance is moderate (recall@1 around 44-45% even with the best model), and the paper's qualitative defense of this number in Appendix C is somewhat hand-wavy; a stronger analysis of why instance identity is hard to recover would be valuable.

Several ablations are missing or thin: no sensitivity analysis for the loss weight λ, no comparison to alternative contrastive formulations (e.g., InfoNCE/CLIP-style softmax) or to other alignment strategies (e.g., weight-space symmetry canonicalization), and no analysis of the parameter-graph size/computational cost of the GMN encoder, which grows with grid resolution.

The 'first framework' claims rest on a narrow definition of the task; related hybrid-field processing and weight-space embedding works could have been positioned more carefully, and the significance of the contribution is bounded by the niche status of object-centric NeRF datasets.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the first architecture-agnostic framework for processing NeRF weights, addressing a genuine limitation of prior work (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) that is tied to specific architectures.

Novel and sensible parameter graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables, with a convincing complexity analysis (Appendix A) showing it is far more memory-efficient than the voxel-grid-based alternative.

Thorough experimental design: 13 architectures across three families, ablations over loss terms (LR, LR+C, LC), multi- vs. single-architecture settings, evaluation on unseen architectural variations, and a cross-dataset generalization test with ObjaNeRF queries.

The analysis of the interplay between rendering and contrastive objectives (Section 4.1, Fig. 3) is insightful and well-supported: rendering loss alone clusters embeddings by architecture, and the SigLIP term fixes this for cross-architecture retrieval, as confirmed quantitatively in Tables 2, 4, 6, and 10.

The framework also outperforms specialized single-architecture baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) in their own settings (Table 3, Table 5), demonstrating the approach is not just more general but also competitive.
Reproducibility details are good: full architecture hyperparameters (Tables 1, 7), training configurations, and hardware details are provided.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework is largely a combination of existing components — the GMN encoder from Lim et al. [23], the nf2vec decoder, and the SigLIP loss from Zhai et al. [39]. The core contributions reduce to the hash-table graph conversion and the observation that a contrastive term helps, both relatively straightforward.

The contrastive objective requires each object to be represented by NeRFs of multiple different architectures (paired data), which is a strong practical assumption for real-world deployment; the paper does not discuss how the method would handle datasets where such pairing is unavailable, nor whether the contrastive loss could be replaced by, e.g., architecture-conditional augmentations.

Evaluation is confined to synthetic ShapenetRender (single dataset, 13 classes) with relatively simple downstream tasks (classification and instance retrieval). Retrieval performance is low in absolute terms (recall@1 of 5.3% for ALL/ALL, 27.2% at k=10), which somewhat weakens the claim of a practically useful embedding space; the qualitative justification in Appendix E partially mitigates this but is not quantified.

No scalability analysis of the encoder on large hash tables: the parameter graph of a multi-resolution hash table has NTF edges (e.g., 4 × 4096 × 2 = 32k edges per table for HASH), and the paper does not report graph sizes, memory footprint, or inference time, despite this being central to the claimed memory-efficiency motivation.

Generalization to unseen architectures is only demonstrated within the three architecture families seen at training time; truly novel architectures (e.g., different graph topologies entirely) are not tested, which limits the strength of the 'architecture-agnostic' claim.
The mixing weight λ = 2×10⁻² is chosen to balance loss magnitudes rather than via a sensitivity study; no ablation over λ is reported.
No mention of code or dataset release, which is important given that a new HASH dataset of NeRFs is created.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and clearly positioned: existing NeRF weight-processing frameworks (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) are tied to a single fixed architecture, and the paper presents the first framework attempting to handle diverse NeRF architectures.

The proposed parameter graph conversion for multi-resolution hash tables is a concrete technical contribution, with a sensible memory-efficiency argument (N(T+F) nodes/NTF edges vs. O(NR^3)) over a naive voxel-grid analogy, and enables processing hash-based NeRFs for the first time.

The empirical analysis of the rendering loss vs. contrastive loss (Fig. 3, Sections 4.1) is informative: the observation that the rendering loss alone clusters embeddings by architecture is a useful finding, and the SigLIP-based contrastive term is a reasonable remedy.

Experiments are extensive in scope: 13 architectures across three families, both seen and unseen hyperparameter variations, single- and multi-architecture settings, classification and retrieval tasks, plus a cross-dataset (ObjaNeRF) generalization check, with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility.
The method outperforms prior single-architecture baselines (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) in their own settings (Table 3, Table 5), showing the approach is competitive even in the restricted scenario.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core components are all borrowed — the GMN encoder from Lim et al. [23], the decoder and rendering loss from nf2vec [38], and the SigLIP loss from Zhai et al. [39]. The main new ingredient is applying this combination to NeRFs and one new graph conversion rule, which feels more like an application/engineering contribution than a fundamental advance.

The claimed 'architecture-agnostic' generalization is narrow: unseen architectures are only hyperparameter variations within the three families seen at training time (different layer counts, dimensions, resolutions). There is no evidence of generalization to genuinely novel architecture families, which the introduction's motivation implies.

Evaluation is confined to ShapenetRender, a small synthetic dataset with 13 classes, except for one qualitative ObjaNeRF experiment. No large-scale or real-world NeRF data is evaluated, weakening the significance and external validity of the claims.

Absolute retrieval performance is modest: recall@1 for cross-architecture instance retrieval is at best ~30% (MLP/TRI) and often ~10-15%, and recall@10 in the ALL/ALL setting is only 27%. The paper argues qualitative results look fine, but the quantitative instance-level results undermine the 'robust performance' claim.

There is no comparison against a simple rendering-based baseline (rendering views + off-the-shelf 3D/image encoder), despite the introduction criticizing this 'naive solution' — it is unclear whether weight-space processing is actually the better route in this diverse-architecture setting.

Several results expose fragility that is not well analyzed: e.g., HASH-11T accuracy drops to ~25-29% across all settings, and cross-family generalization varies erratically (TRI-16W vs TRI-8C behave oppositely). The paper offers only speculative post-hoc explanations.
The single hyperparameter lambda is set so the two loss terms have 'similar magnitude' — a weak justification; no sensitivity analysis or ablation over lambda is provided.
No mention of code release, and training takes ~2 weeks on an A6000, which limits reproducibility and practical adoption.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated novelty: this is the first framework to process NeRFs with diverse architectures by operating directly on their weights, and the first to handle hash-table-parameterized NeRFs, which are the most widely adopted NeRF family in practice.

The technical contribution is sensible and well-integrated: extending Lim et al.'s parameter graph formulation to multi-resolution hash tables is a non-trivial and well-justified design (the paper convincingly analyzes the memory efficiency argument, N(T+F) vs O(N(R^3+F))), and the SigLIP-based contrastive objective is a natural and effective remedy for the architecture-cluster problem they empirically identify.

Comprehensive and well-structured experiments: 13 architectures across three families, both single- and multi-architecture settings, seen and unseen architectures, classification and instance-level retrieval, plus ablation over the three loss configurations (L_R, L_R+C, L_C) with consistent explanations linking latent space structure (t-SNE analysis) to downstream behavior.

Honest reporting of limitations and failure modes (e.g., TRI-8C, TRI-16W, HASH-11T anomalies, weak LR retrieval results), and a genuinely useful empirical insight that rendering and contrastive objectives serve complementary purposes (class separability vs. architecture invariance).

The paper outperforms prior single-architecture methods (nf2vec, Cardace et al.) in the settings where they are applicable, providing evidence that the approach is not only more general but also competitive.
Detailed appendices (architecture tables, hyperparameters, training details, extended results) support reproducibility, and the implementation builds on public codebases.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single synthetic dataset (ShapenetRender) with limited scale (~31k training NeRFs); generalization to real-world or large-scale NeRF datasets is only touched via a small qualitative Objaverse experiment. The authors acknowledge this, but it weakens claims of practical applicability.

The contrastive objective requires architecture-paired data: every object must be represented by multiple NeRF architectures at training time. This is a significant practical constraint that is not deeply discussed as a limitation, and no experiment tests the framework when architecture pairing is partial or unavailable.

Absolute instance-level retrieval performance is modest (recall@1 of 5.3% ALL/ALL, up to ~30-59% only for the best cross-architecture combinations at k=5-10), and the ALL/ALL case is close to uninformative; qualitative results partially offset this, but the headline retrieval numbers are weak.

Generalization to unseen architectures is uneven: significant accuracy drops for TRI-16W, TRI-8C, and especially HASH-11T (~25-29% regardless of training set), suggesting the 'architecture-agnostic' claim holds only within a fairly narrow band of hyperparameter perturbations.

The method is largely a composition of existing components (GMN from Lim et al., nf2vec decoder, SigLIP loss); while the combination and the hash-table graph conversion are new, the technical depth is limited and no theoretical analysis of why the contrastive term fixes the architecture clustering is provided.

Hyperparameter choices (e.g., lambda = 2e-2 to match loss magnitudes, t and b initialization) are empirical and no sensitivity analysis is given; also, comparison against a GMN trained with simpler alignment losses (e.g., InfoNCE instead of SigLIP, or a simple alignment penalty) is missing to justify the specific design.
The main tables lack error bars / multiple seeds, so the significance of differences of a few percentage points (common in Tables 2-4) is unclear.
